text: Good news; your blood work including your white blood cells, platelets, and liver and kidney function are all normal. Since the infection and organ failure possibilities are off the table, can you tell me more about the appearance of the rash—specifically, does it itch, hurt, or change when you press on it?

speaker: Patient
text: 47-year-old male. The patient presents with a rash that started last night, finding it very concerning. He does not recall being exposed to any new environmental stimuli such as detergents or plants like poison ivy. He mentions he recently started seeing a primary care provider for arthritis management and a new onset cough.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That new cough is a significant detail; has it been productive, and does it occur more at night? Also, regarding the arthritis medication you recently started, what is the specific name of the drug?

REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray
REQUEST TEST: ANA, Rheumatoid_Factor

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Chest_X-Ray: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no infiltrates, masses, or pleural effusions; ANA: Negative; Rheumatoid_Factor: Negative

speaker: Doctor
text:
The chest X-ray is clear and your autoimmune markers are negative, so pneumonia and systemic lupus are unlikely. While the medication name you started for arthritis isn't clear yet, can you describe exactly what the rash looks like—is it flat or raised, and does it spread? Also, do you have any joint pain or swelling in your hands or feet?

REQUEST TEST: Skin_Biopsy

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Skin_Biopsy: Epidermal necrosis and detachment, consistent with severe drug reaction.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).

The skin biopsy confirms severe drug reaction with epidermal necrosis. Given your recent start of arthritis medication, this is likely a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR) such as SJS or TEN, potentially caused by drugs like sulfonamides or anticonvulsants used for arthritis. You need to stop the offending agent immediately and be admitted for supportive care.
